study_type.claude: Mixed methods (sequential exploratory: survey + semi-structured interviews)
study_type.nlm: Mixed methods (sequential exploratory: quantitative survey + qualitative semi-structured interviews)

research_method.claude: Sequential exploratory mixed methods: large-scale survey on the DX platform (two AI-assistant items) + 11 semi-structured interviews with inductive open coding and descriptive thematic analysis; Pearson correlation satisfaction x time savings (N = 2754)
research_method.nlm: Sequential exploratory mixed methods: quantitative survey (2,989 respondents, DX platform, satisfaction and perceived time savings) + 11 qualitative semi-structured interviews; Pearson r = 0.34
research_method.value: Sequential exploratory mixed-methods design: large-scale company survey on the DX platform (two AI-assistant items: satisfaction and perceived weekly time savings with GitHub Copilot; 2989 respondents; Pearson correlation between the two items) followed by 11 semi-structured interviews analysed with inductive open coding and descriptive thematic analysis; six-factor framework with proposed survey questions
research_method.note: Section 4.1 reports 2898 engineers answering at least one item (Claude flags the 2989/2898 inconsistency; NotebookLM uses both figures).

context.claude: Industry; BNY Mellon (financial company), developers with GitHub Copilot access; ~8000 engineers answered the general survey, 2989 the analysed items; 11 interviewees (early career, mid career, management; backend/full-stack/frontend)
context.nlm: Industry; financial services enterprise BNY Mellon; 2,989 survey respondents and 11 interview participants
context.value: industry; BNY Mellon (financial services), developers with access to GitHub Copilot; 2989 survey respondents (of ~8000 engineers who took the company survey) and 11 interviewees across seniority levels and roles
context.note: ~8000 figure reported by Claude, mentioned by NotebookLM only in limitations (not contradicted).

dora_applied.note: Referenced only: Factor 3 compared with DORA throughput metrics (Table 3, Section 5.2).

space_applied.note: Referenced only: Factors 2 and 4 compared with SPACE dimensions (Table 3).

ai_discussed.note: GitHub Copilot (LLM coding assistant) is the object of study.

remote_covid.note: Work mode not reported by either; interviews were merely conducted virtually via Teams.

data_window.note: Not stated by either (survey and interview dates not given).

cat_productivity.note: Factor 3 rate of task completion/throughput; perceived time savings (self-reported).

cat_quality.note: Thin basis: quality of task completion and 'bugs avoided' in Factor 3; review quality in Factor 4 (both extractors tag peer review as Quality/Collaboration).

cat_collaboration.note: Factor 4 ease of peer review (review comments, reviewer-author trust).

cat_satisfaction.note: General satisfaction (CSAT) survey item; Factor 2 frustration.

cat_activity.note: Not measured: commit frequency, code completion acceptance and LOC are discussed (Sections 4.2, 5.1) and LOC is one suggested margin in Factor 3; acceptance rates could not be obtained.

cat_delivery.note: Agreed Yes but not confirmed in the full text: both tag Factor 3 (rate of task completion, a productivity measure) as Delivery; deployment frequency and lead time appear only in the DORA comparison (Section 5.2).

cat_devex.note: Borderline: both say the DX survey platform/framework (Greiler, Storey & Noda 2022) was applied, but only as the vehicle for two items (satisfaction, time savings); Noda/Storey/Forsgren DevEx dimensions are not operationalized. Cognitive load (Factor 2) comes from interviews and is mapped to SPACE.

cat_agile.note: NotebookLM mentions 'sprint tracking' only as a possible collection method for Factor 3; no process metric.

cat_survey.note: Survey items (satisfaction, perceived time savings), interviews on perceptions, proposed survey questions per factor (Table 2).

evidence.quote: We employed a sequential exploratory mixed-methods research design [11] involving two phases.
At BNY Mellon, we conduct a survey with 2989 developer responses and 11 in-depth interviews.
To answer RQ2, we conducted inductive open coding and applied a descriptive thematic analysis of all responses to the questions about perceptions on productivity metrics.
The survey was completed by around 8000 total engineers throughout the company.
Regarding our particular questions, we had 2989 respondents—which is a majority of engineers who have access to GitHub Copilot
This study analyzes the validity of different approaches to evaluating the productivity impacts of AI coding assistants by leveraging mixed-method research.
(1) General satisfaction [15, 42]: Consumer Satisfaction score for GitHub Copilot.
(2) Perceived time savings [26]: On average, how much time is saved with GitHub Copilot per week?
Do AI tools improve the rates of and quality of task completion?
Many participants noted the importance of measuring throughout (P5,9,11)—i.e., the rate at which individual or teams can complete a well-defined task
By what measurable margin (time saved, lines of code written, bugs avoided) do tasks complete faster?
Does the use of AI affect trust between reviewers and authors?
evidence.loc: PDF p. 7 (Table 2, Ease of peer review)

evidence.quote: How often do developers experience frustration due to irrelevant, incorrect, or repetitive AI suggestions?
Commit frequency and code completion acceptance are frequently used to measure a developer’s usage of AI coding assistants.
evidence.loc: PDF p. 8 (5.1 Operationalizing AI productivity factors)

evidence.quote: Using simple metrics like the number of lines of code written does not necessarily correlate with impact.
